comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm Nikita, and this is Tiden, the product we've been building for the past year. It's for engineering teams shipping agent-written code every day who want to let agents do the coding while keeping control of what ships.Qase is a software testing platform used by tens of thousands of builders, and 9 years of building it for them taught us a lot about how quality work gets done. Last year that changed on our own team: agents started producing most of the code, and the rest of our process didn't speed up with it. Review, testing, release, keeping requirements current: all of it became bottlenecks.Other engineering teams tell the same story. A gaming publisher I talked to, with about 1k+ developers, saw pull request volume go up 4 to 5 times while the number of features they shipped stayed flat. A payments company described 10 times the coding output and 10% more delivery.The problem underneath itAn agent session produces the code, the tests that pass on that code, and the docs describing what it built. The next session reads those docs as fact. Every artifact agrees with every other one, because they all came from the same place. A QA automation lead at a tax and accounting platform put it best: "If you have an agent that decides what to build, and then another agent is grading what's being built against what was actually built, you're essentially encoding the wrong thing. Your tests will pass, they'll be green, but it wasn’t what you wanted."The two usual fixes, another rules file in the repo and better AI code review, both sit inside that same loop. The judge has to sit outside it.What Tiden doesTiden is that judge. It's intent verification for coding agents: it sits beside your agents, whichever ones you use, and verifies that what they built is what you actually asked for. It keeps that intent as specs, versioned like code, and checks every change against them rather than against the session that produced it.Every agent session becomes a closed loop:A session hook captures what you asked for before the first editThe change comes back as a requirement for you to review; requirements branch and merge like codeTiden picks the tests the change touches, runs them in your environment, and the agent fixes what fails before anything mergesThe gate is tied to the spec. Red tells the agent what to fix. Green is a pass you can defend, with the evidence attachedIn production, an error traces back to the release, the change and the prompt behind it, and the fix comes with the test that was missingTiden works beside Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Copilot, and belongs to none of them. Specs live as one versioned record every agent reads from, instead of a growing pile of markdown. You set the thresholds and the gates, and a person approves anything the loop can't settle.One limit, stated plainly: Tiden checks the work against what you asked for. Whether you asked for the right thing is still a human judgment.Get startedTiden is live at https://tiden.ai. The CLI installs in one command, the docs are at https://docs.tiden.ai, and Starter and Team both come with a 14-day free trial. If you'd rather talk to us first, there's a short form on the site: https://tiden.ai/contact.What I'd like from youHonest feedback over upvotes. Where does your team feel this gap most: review, regression, release, or production? What would make you trust an external check?

week.name: Onepin

week.description: AI voices sound human now. But they still guess names from the spelling, and nobody has time to listen to every line. Onepin checks how a name was said, not just what the transcript spells. And there is no box where you type phonetic spellings: the dictionary and the fix do that work, so your script stays as written.Built for anyone shipping AI voiceover at volume: product videos, ads, explainers, dubbing, audiobooks, courses, and platforms that put a voice in front of millions of users. comments.text: Hi Product Hunt community, I’m Bharath, founder of Inferock.Every team running LLMs in production pays for calls that came back empty, truncated, timed out, or returned broken JSON. You usually find out from a user, and you can’t prove it to anyone.Inferock sits between your app and the provider and measures every call against a published baseline for quality, speed and cost. month.name: Jev
month.tagline: Fast, structured AI decisions for software automation
month.description: Jev is TypeSafe AI's System One frontier model: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out. month.name: Voiskey
month.tagline: AI voice typing that sounds right in every app
month.description: Voiskey starts from what you meant, not just what you said. Speak a rough thought and it comes back shaped for where it's going and who's reading it: casual with a friend, composed with a colleague, technical with an AI. It arrives 5x faster than typing, cleaned up and ready to send, while you still sound like you. Voiskey is now available on iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows, in over 100 languages. comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm Jenny, from the Voiskey team. We started this because of the same wall we kept hitting - AI dictation still isn't truly edit-free. The text comes out polished, and a lot of the time sanded flat: a message to a friend comes back like a memo, or a note to a colleague comes back like a template. None of it sounds like you, so you have to go back in and manually re-edit it before you send it. That's what Voiskey is built around. We called it "expression intelligence". Voiskey doesn't just catching your words. It works out what you meant, who's going to read it, and how you'd have put it yourself. The polish moves. Your voice stays. Why Voiskey: * Fits the moment. Reads the situation you're writing into and adjusts how the text comes out. * Keeps your voice. Your slang, your shorthand, and your way of putting things stay. * Learns your words. Remembers the names and terms you correct, so you fix them once. * Translates as you speak. Say it in your language, send it in theirs. It reads native, not translated. * Ask AI. Say what you want written and it lands in the field. Ask a question and the answer opens in a window. It's free to try, and there's a free month of Pro during launch. We'd love to hear what you think!

month.name: Rill Browser
month.tagline: The browser where Claude Code and Codex work beside you
month.description: Rill is an AI-native browser built around the Claude Code and Codex you already use. Browse normally, then press ⌘E on any page to turn what you're looking at into a task for your agent. Rill finds the right project, passes along the context, and the agent works while you keep browsing. comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm William! I made Rill because I want to always stay in the flow. As an ADHD, I never liked code-switching. It's a browser with your Claude Code or Codex working alongside you. When something on a page gives you an idea, you say so right there, and an agent starts on it in the right project. You don't have to spend time looking for the right folder, rephrasing everything you just saw on the web, and you don't switch in and out of work mode. The work goes on with you in the flow.This matters now more than ever. Agents have shortened the distance between ideas to output near zero. So the bottleneck is capturing the idea at the moment you have it. That moment is nearly always while you're taking something in, and that is what a browser is for.Rill is a free AI-native browser. It's WebKit-based, which means it's native to Mac. Full disclosure — I'm a big fan of Anthropic and actually built an app that works exclusively with Claude Desktop for secure local file search. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
